courses.repertoire: As White: the Giuoco Pianissimo, with c3, d3 and a slow build-up. As Black: 3...Bc5, then ...Nf6, ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7.
courses.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4: the bishop aims at f7, the weakest square near Black's king.

why.text:
As White, the Italian follows the opening principles: develop quickly, castle early, and aim the bishop at f7, the square only Black's king defends. The slow Giuoco Pianissimo taught here avoids the long forcing lines of the open game, so one plan works against almost everything. The opening goes back to Greco in the 1620s, and top players have favored it since the Berlin Defense blunted the Ruy Lopez in Kramnik's 2000 world title match.

As Black, 3...Bc5 is the most natural reply: the bishop takes its best diagonal and aims at f2, just as White's aims at f7. It avoids the sharp 4.Ng5 lines of the Two Knights Defense, and in most games you can copy White's quiet setup. Only the Center attack and the Evans Gambit need exact moves.

rows: 4.c3 and 5.d3, castle, Re1. Drop the bishop to b3 before ...Na5 or ...b5 can trade it.
4.d3, not 4.Ng5. 4...Bc5 5.c3 is the main line. Against ...Na5, Bb5, Ba4 and Bc2 keep the bishop.
4...Nf6, then ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7. Against 5.d4, take with the bishop: 5...Bxd4.
5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+, then ...d5. Against 7.Nc3, take the e4 pawn.
4...Nf6 and ...d6. Against 5.Bg5, ...h6 and, if needed, ...g5 before you castle.
4...Bxb4 5.c3 Ba5, then give the pawn back with ...d5.
4...Nf6, ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7. The fork trick 5.Nxe5? fails to 6...Nxc4!

courses.repertoire: Advance (Short system), plus the Two Knights and the Fantasy
courses.summary: Gain space with 3.e5, castle before anything sharp, and meet ...c5 calmly. The Two Knights and the Fantasy are trap-filled surprise weapons.
overview: Learn one system first. The Advance (3.e5) is the main weapon; the Two Knights (2.Nc3 and 3.Nf3) and the Fantasy (3.f3) are surprise weapons full of traps.
In the Advance, the pawn on e5 gains space and keeps Black's knight off f6. Develop calmly with Nf3, Be2 and O-O before anything sharp.
The main line, 3...Bf5 4.Nf3 e6, comes up in more than half of your Advance games.
Black's counterplay is ...c5 against d4, the base of your pawn chain. Guard d4 with Be3; against an early 3...c5, take with 4.dxc5.
In the Two Knights, wait before playing d4. Ask Black's bishop the question with h3 and take the bishop pair. After 4...Nf6, 5.Qe2 sets the smothered-mate trap.
In the Fantasy, the f-pawn holds e4. If Black takes, fxe4 gives you two center pawns and the half-open f-file, but your king is looser, so develop fast and castle.

courses.summary: Get the c8 bishop out before ...e6, hit d4 against the Advance, and know the traps in the Fantasy and Karpov lines.
overview: The idea of the Caro-Kann: support ...d5 with the c-pawn, and get the c8 bishop out before ...e6 shuts it in.

Learn three structures first: the Advance (3.e5), the Classical (3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2) and the Exchange (exd5 cxd5), which comes from both 2.d4 and 2.Nf3. Together they come up in more than half of your games.
Against the Advance (3.e5), hit the base of White's chain at once with 3...c5. Against 4.c3, take on d4 and pile up on it with ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...Nf5.
Against 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2, take on e4 and play 4...Bf5. Answer h4 with ...h6, and trade the light-squared bishops calmly.
In the Exchange, develop with ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...e6, then play for the minority attack with ...b5 and ...b4. Against the Panov's isolated d-pawn, blockade d5 and trade pieces.
Know the traps: in the Fantasy, 5.dxe5? runs into ...Qh4+; in the Karpov, 5.Qe2 Ngf6?? allows 6.Nd6 mate.

courses.repertoire: As White: the Advance (3.e5), with 6.a3 in the main line. As Black: ...c5 against the Advance, ...Nc6 and ...Bd6 in the Exchange, and the Rubinstein (3...dxe4) against 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2.
courses.summary: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5: Black builds a solid center and hits back with ...c5.

why.text:
As White, the Advance gives you space and one clear plan, with much less theory to learn than after 3.Nc3, where Black chooses between the Winawer, the Classical and the Rubinstein.

As Black, the French gives you a solid position and the same counterattack against almost every White setup: hit White's center from the side with ...c5.

rows: Advance main line: 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Qb6 (also 4...Qb6 5.Nf3 Nc6)
Play 6.a3 and b4. After 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, Nc3 and Na4 chase the queen. Count the attackers before Black takes on d4.
Develop with ...Nc6, ...Bd6, ...Bg4 and ...Nge7, then castle short. Against 4.Nc3, put the knight on f6 to guard d5.
Hit d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Against 6.a3, lock the queenside with 6...c4. Against the Milner-Barry Gambit, 6.Bd3, play ...Bd7 before ...Nxd4.
Play ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6 to trade White's knight on e4, then free your game with ...c5.
Play 6.Be2 and castle. Avoid 6.Bb5?, which runs into 6...Nxe5!
Early ...cxd4 and the Wade Variation: 4...cxd4, or 4...Qb6 5.Nf3 Bd7
Against 5...Bb4+, block with 6.Nc3. Against the Wade, trade bishops with 6.Be2 Bb5 7.Bxb5+ Qxb5 and hit the queen with 8.Na3.

courses.repertoire: As White: the Exchange Variation and the minority attack. As Black: the Tartakower Variation.
courses.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6: Black declines the pawn and holds d5 with the e-pawn.

why.text:
As Black, 2...e6 holds the center with a pawn and keeps the position solid. The cost is the c8 bishop, shut in behind e6, so Black's plans are about freeing it.

As White, taking on d5 early fixes the pawn structure. You know your plans in advance, and there are few early tactics to calculate.

rows: Play Bg5, e3, Bd3 and Qc2, and castle. Then the minority attack (Rb1, b4, b5), or Nge2, f3 and e4.
Play ...Be7 and castle. Against 5.Bf4, hit the center with ...c5. Against 5.Bg5, play ...h6 and the Tartakower.
The Tartakower: ...Be7, castle, ...h6, then ...b6 and ...Bb7. If White takes on f6, take back with the bishop.
5.e4 gains time on the knight and builds a full center.
Take on d5 anyway. With no knight on f6 to pin, the bishop goes to f4.
Play 5...Nbd7, which sets the Elephant trap. Then ...c6, ...Be7, castle, ...Re8 and ...Nf8.

courses.repertoire: As White: 3.Nf3 and 4.Nc3, then cxd5 and Bg5 against ...e6. As Black: the Czech Variation (4...dxc4 5.a4 Bf5).
courses.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6: Black guards d5 with the c-pawn.

why.text:
As Black, ...c6 guards d5 and keeps the c8 bishop's diagonal open, so the bishop can come out before ...e6 shuts it in. Solid, with a few exact lines to know.

As White, the Slav often turns into positions you know from the Declined, so the same plans work.

rows: Take on d5, then Bg5, Bd3, Qc2, castle and the minority attack, as in the Exchange Variation.
Take on c4. Against 5.a4, play the Czech Variation: ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bb4 and castle. Against 5.e4 or 5.e3, keep the pawn with 5...b5.
Take on d5 and play Qb3, which hits b7. ...b6? and ...Qd7? lose material.
Copy White's setup: ...Nf6, ...Nc6, ...Bf5 and ...e6. Watch for Qb3 hitting b7.
Play ...Bf5 at once, then ...e6, ...Nbd7 and ...Be7, and castle.
Take on c4 and hold the pawn with ...b5. After 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.e4 b5, 6.a4? loses material to 6...b4!

courses.repertoire: As White: 3.e3 and Bxc4. As Black: ...e5 at once, and the Classical setup against 3.Nf3.
courses.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4: Black takes the pawn and gives up the center for a moment.

why.text:
As Black, giving up the center for a moment frees your pieces, and you get to hit back at White's center early. White wins the pawn back, but you develop quickly.

As White, you win the pawn back at once and keep the center, with a small, safe edge.

rows: Against 4.d5, play ...Nf6. After 5.e4, 5...b5! keeps the extra pawn. Never play ...Bb4 while Qa4+ is possible.
After 4.Bxc4 exd4 5.exd4, White has an isolated pawn: play ...Nf6, ...Bd6 and castle, then ...Nc6 and ...Bg4.
Against 4.d5, play ...Nf6 and ...b5, as against 3.Nc3. Against 4.Nf3, take on d4, then ...Nc6 and ...Be6.
4.Bxc4 and castle. Then trade queens for a small endgame edge, or keep them and push e4.
4.a4 hits the pawn chain. After 4...c6 5.axb5 cxb5, 6.Qf3 wins a piece.
After 4.Bxc4 exd4 5.exd4, play Nf3 and Nc3, castle, and use the open e-file.

rows: Rubinstein System: 4.cxd5 exd5, then Nf3, g3 and Bg2
The bishop on g2 hits d5, the isolated pawn. Castle and keep up the pressure.
Play ...Nc6 and ...Nf6. If White develops the f1 bishop before taking on d5, take on c4, then play ...a6, ...b5 and ...Bb7.
Develop with ...Nc6, ...Nf6 and ...Be7, and castle. Avoid needless trades.
Push ...d4! and win the pawn back later. Never 5...Bxc5?: 6.Qxd5 wins your d5 pawn.
Take the pawn with Qxd4 and keep it.

courses.repertoire: As White: Classical (5.Nf3, 6.Be2 and castling), with 9.b4 against the Mar del Plata. As Black: the Kazakh 6...Na6 against the Classical, and ...c5 against the Four Pawns and the Sämisch.
courses.summary: As White: develop naturally, castle, and let Black commit first. Close the center with d5 and race on the queenside with b4 and c5; against ...exd4, guard e4 with f3 and use your space. As Black: let White build the big center, castle behind the g7 bishop, then strike with ...e5 or ...c5. The Kazakh 6...Na6 and a knight on c5 keep the theory light against the Classical.
overview: As White: play the Classical: 5.Nf3, 6.Be2 and castle. You make no weakening pawn moves, so Black's attack has nothing to aim at until the center closes.

As White: after 6.Be2, Black's main reply is 6...e5, in about a third of those games, and 6...Nbd7 or 6...Nc6 usually lead to ...e5 as well. Castle first, then close the center with d5 or hold it with Be3.
As White: against 7...Nc6, the Mar del Plata, play 8.d5 and 9.b4. Your queenside attack with c5 must arrive before Black's ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5.
As White: against 7...exd4 8.Nxd4 Re8, guard e4 with 9.f3 at once. Natural moves such as 9.Bg5? or 9.Re1? let Black take on e4.
As White: against 6...c5, castle and take back on d4 with the knight. Your pawns on c4 and e4 form the Maroczy Bind, which clamps d5 and Black's freeing breaks.
As White: know the tricks: 5...e5?! 6.dxe5 wins a pawn before Black has castled, and the fork trick 8...Nxe4?? fails because your queen guards d4.
As Black: set up with ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6 and ...O-O, then strike at White's center with ...e5 or ...c5. Your king is safe behind the g7 bishop.

As Black: White's systems are spread out: 5.Nf3 comes up in about a sixth of your games, and the Four Pawns, the Sämisch, the Makogonov, 5.Be2 and 5.Bd3 in about 5 to 8% each. Learn the plan for each.
As Black: against the Classical, 6.Be2, play 6...Na6 and ...e5. When White closes the center with d5, put the knight on c5, play ...a5 so b4 can't chase it, then ...f5.
As Black: against the Four Pawns (5.f4) and the Sämisch (5.f3 and Be3), strike at once with ...c5. White's center is loose and the king is not castled yet.
As Black: against the Averbakh (Be2 and Bg5), play ...Na6 before ...e5. Otherwise Nd5 hits f6 and c7 and wins the exchange.
As Black: against 6.Bd3, play 6...Bg4 and pile up on d4 with ...Bxf3, ...Nc6 and ...Nd7. The natural Ne2?? then loses material to ...Nce5.

surveys.summary: 1.d4 usually leads to slower, more strategic games than 1.e4. Against 1...d5, White can skip the Queen's Gambit and play a system such as the London or the Colle: the same setup in almost every game, so they are easy to remember. The London is one of the most popular choices at club level (and works against 1...Nf6 too); the Colle is much rarer and is listed with the uncommon replies. Against 1...Nf6 2.c4, Black plays the King's Indian in about a quarter of club games: Black lets White build a big center, then hits it with ...e5 or ...c5 and attacks on the kingside.

surveys.summary: Each opening has one board and a Watch button for each of Black's main replies, played out to move 4 along the moves club players choose most often on Lichess. Under each board, White's plan and Black's plan are summed up in a few lines. No course is planned for these openings yet.

rows: White controls d5 from the side and often fianchettoes with g3 and Bg2. Positional games; after 1...e5 it is a Sicilian with colors reversed.
The most flexible first move: White develops, stops ...e5 and chooses a setup later. It usually turns into a 1.d4 opening, the English or the Réti.
White grabs e5 with the f-pawn: a Dutch Defense with colors reversed. Kingside attacking chances, at some cost to king safety.
White fianchettoes the queen's bishop toward e5 and plays against Black's center from the side. Offbeat, maneuvering games.
White fianchettoes the king's bishop and decides on the center later, often reaching a King's Indian Attack or an English. Slow and flexible.
table.note: Share: how often each first move starts a game, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. For comparison, 1.e4 starts 62% of these games and 1.d4 26%.
